Born to Cruise, Ready to Tour

Cruisers and touring go together like a full tank and an empty road. The relaxed riding position, torquey engines and low seat height that define the breed are exactly the traits that make long days a pleasure. Some cruisers arrive tour-ready from the factory, others need a few thoughtful additions, but all of them share a laid-back character perfectly suited to soaking up Britain's landscapes at an unhurried pace. Whether you ride a full-dress Honda Gold Wing, a bagger like the Harley-Davidson Road Glide, or the mighty Triumph Rocket 3 GT, this guide will help you get the best from it on tour.

Two Very Different Starting Points

Cruisers split into two camps for touring. Full-dress and bagger models such as the Gold Wing and Road Glide come with fairings, hard luggage and often heated grips and audio built in. For these bikes, touring prep is mostly about fine-tuning what you already have. Stripped-back cruisers and power cruisers like the Rocket 3 need more of the kit added, but reward you with unmistakable style and, in the Rocket's case, a wall of torque that makes overtaking on the A82 utterly effortless.

Luggage: Style Meets Capacity

If your cruiser already has hard panniers, use them and add a top box for helmets and soft kit. A Givi Monokey Top Box 45L swallows a full-face lid and doubles as a comfortable backrest for a pillion. For custom and power cruisers without factory luggage, throwover-style bags keep the classic look while adding real capacity. I like the SW-Motech Legend Gear Saddlebags for their waxed-canvas retro looks that suit a cruiser far better than modern textile.

On a cruiser, luggage is part of the aesthetic. Choose bags that complement the bike's lines and you get practicality without spoiling the style that made you buy it.

Cruisers with their long wheelbase and generous subframes carry weight beautifully and are barely affected by loaded panniers. For fitting support frames and heat-shielding bags away from those big exhausts, see our luggage mounting guide.

Wind Protection: The Fairing Question

Faired baggers and the Gold Wing already offer excellent weather protection, one of the great joys of touring on them through a Scottish downpour. For a naked cruiser or power cruiser, a windscreen or batwing fairing transforms long-distance comfort. A Memphis Shades Batwing Fairing looks the part and takes the wind off your chest, turning a bike that gets tiring above 60mph into one you can ride all day. If you prefer a simpler bolt-on screen, our motorcycle windscreen guide will help you pick the right height so airflow lifts cleanly over your helmet rather than buffeting it.

Comfort and Ergonomics

The cruiser riding position, feet forward and back upright, is superb for cruising but can put pressure on your tailbone over a very long day because you cannot easily shift your weight. The classic upgrades are:

  • A seat cushion. An Airhawk Cruiser Seat Cushion uses air cells to spread pressure and eliminates the numb-backside problem on 400-mile days.
  • Heated grips. If yours are not factory-fitted, Oxford Heaterz Cruiser Heated Grips made for larger cruiser bars are a cheap, transformative addition for British spring and autumn touring.
  • Highway pegs let you stretch your legs and change position on a long motorway drone, which does wonders for hip comfort.
  • An intercom. A Sena 50S Intercom is ideal on a cruiser, letting you enjoy music and navigation prompts at the relaxed pace these bikes encourage.

Range and Fuel Strategy

Cruisers vary wildly here. A Gold Wing carries a huge tank and will cross most of Scotland on a single fill, while a big power cruiser worked hard through the twisties can be thirstier than you expect. The Rocket 3's enormous engine is surprisingly relaxed at a cruise but drinks quickly if you use its ferocious midrange. As always, on remote routes like the NC500 or the empty roads around the Welsh A44, fill up at every opportunity rather than trusting the range readout. The relaxed cruiser pace naturally favours economy, so ride smoothly and you will be pleasantly surprised.

Pace: The Cruiser Sweet Spot

Cruisers reward a flowing, unhurried style. They are not built to be hustled through tight hairpins like a naked bike, though a power cruiser will surprise people on a fast A-road. The magic of cruiser touring is the ability to settle into a rhythm and let the miles roll by. A run down the A82 alongside Loch Lomond, or a gentle exploration of the Lake District passes at a pace that lets you actually look at the scenery, is what these bikes do best. Do not fight the character of the bike by rushing. Slow down, look around, and enjoy the ride.

What to Upgrade First

For a naked cruiser, spend on wind protection first, then a seat cushion, then luggage, then heated grips. For a faired bagger or Gold Wing, you likely need very little beyond a top box and perhaps a seat cushion for the really long days. Buy the bike closest to your touring needs and you save a fortune in accessories.

Honest Limitations

Cruisers are heavy, and low-speed manoeuvres, tight car parks and steep hairpins demand respect, especially two-up and fully loaded. Ground clearance is limited on many cruisers, so you cannot carry the same corner speed as a sportsbike or naked. And the sheer weight of a dressed Gold Wing or Rocket 3 means a drop is a serious business. None of this matters on the open road, where these bikes are in their element.

Who It Suits

Cruiser touring suits the rider who values comfort, presence and a relaxed pace over outright agility. If you want to cover big distances in comfort, carry a pillion in style, and arrive fresh rather than frazzled, a cruiser is hard to beat. For serious two-up touring, the Gold Wing and Road Glide are among the best bikes in the world, and our best touring bikes guide explains why. Whichever cruiser you choose, set it up thoughtfully and Britain's open roads will feel like they were made for it.

Full-dress baggers arrive tour-ready; stripped-back cruisers need luggage, a screen and comfort kit added.
Choose luggage that complements the bike's lines, such as waxed-canvas throwover bags.
A batwing fairing or screen transforms comfort on a naked cruiser above 60mph.
Cruisers reward a flowing, unhurried pace rather than corner-carving.

faq.a: Very. The relaxed feet-forward position, torquey engines and low seat height that define cruisers are exactly the traits that make long days a pleasure. Full-dress models and baggers like the Gold Wing and Road Glide arrive tour-ready with fairings and hard luggage, while stripped-back cruisers reward you with style once you add luggage, a screen and comfort kit. All share a laid-back character suited to soaking up the miles.

faq.q: Do I need a screen on a cruiser?
faq.a: If your cruiser is faired or a full-dress bagger, it already offers excellent weather protection. On a naked cruiser or power cruiser, a windscreen or batwing fairing transforms long-distance comfort, taking the wind off your chest and turning a bike that tires you above 60mph into one you can ride all day. Pick a height so airflow lifts cleanly over your helmet rather than buffeting it.

faq.q: How do I improve cruiser comfort on long days?
faq.a: The feet-forward position is superb for cruising but can pressure your tailbone because you cannot easily shift your weight. Fit an air seat cushion to spread pressure and beat the numb-backside problem, add highway pegs so you can stretch and change leg position, and fit heated grips for British spring and autumn. An intercom suits the relaxed pace, letting you enjoy music and navigation prompts.

faq.q: What are the limitations of touring on a cruiser?
faq.a: Cruisers are heavy, so low-speed manoeuvres, tight car parks and steep hairpins demand respect, especially two-up and loaded. Ground clearance is limited on many models, so you cannot carry the same corner speed as a sportsbike or naked, and a dropped Gold Wing or Rocket 3 is a serious business. None of this matters on the open road, where these bikes are firmly in their element.
